answer:
1. The animation shows a historical comparison of buying and renting. It uses an example buyer who bought a house in April 2012 and was about $484,000 ahead after ten years, compared with someone who rented. A large house stands over rows of smaller houses. The legend says lit houses mean the buyer was ahead after ten years and dark houses mean the renter was ahead. The data sources are listed as FHFA home prices, BLS rents and Freddie Mac rates. The label "ILLUSTRATIVE" is on every frame.

2. The first frames only add a label. The "April 2012" start date appears over the house in frame 2 and stays there. In frames 4 to 6, a stack of money rises beside the house, and the text "about $484,000 ahead" appears. The stack is tallest in frame 5 and about the same in frame 6. A note says all dollar amounts are in dollars of the day. The rows of houses stay the same throughout.

3. It means that for someone who bought in April 2012, owning came out well ahead of renting over the next ten years. That was after the cost of interest, taxes and so on, assuming the animation counted those. Most of the rows of houses look lit, which suggests buying won in most of the starting months shown. A few look darker, so renting won for some starting dates. The footers, "US only · history, not a forecast" and "ILLUSTRATIVE", say this describes the past and is not a prediction.

4. The animation gives no direct advice. A viewer might take away that buying has often paid off over a ten-year stretch in the US. The footer warns against treating that as a promise, and the result depends heavily on the starting date. A viewer would need to check this against their own price, rate, rent and how long they plan to stay.

5. The idea and the $484,000 figure come from the animation's picture and text. The advice in 4 is my own reading. The animation never tells viewers to buy or rent, and it explicitly says it is not a forecast.
